entities.name: Island Records
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Island Records, founded in 1959 in Jamaica by Chris Blackwell — a young Englishman of Jamaican heritage who had been driving around Kingston distributing Jamaican music before establishing a proper label — is one of the most creatively significant record labels in British and global music history, responsible for bringing reggae to the world through Bob Marley and the Wailers, developing U2, Cat Stevens, Robert Palmer, and many other defining artists, and maintaining a distinctive independent creative ethos that shaped rock, reggae, and pop across six decades.

Chris Blackwell's genius was cultural bridging: born into Jamaican landed gentry (his father was a Jamaican planter, his mother was the actress Blanche Lindo), he understood both Jamaican music culture and the British and American markets where it could break through. His 1972 decision to invest in Bob Marley and the Wailers — then a poorly recorded reggae group with limited international profile — and to present them to the rock audience (through rock-venue appearances, rock producer (Jimmy Miller working with them initially), and high-quality album production) transformed Marley from Jamaican star to global superstar and reggae from Jamaican niche to worldwide genre.

Island's rock roster — Traffic, Free, King Crimson, Cat Stevens, Roxy Music, and the defining relationship with U2 from Boy (1980) through the mega-success of The Joshua Tree (1987) and beyond — made it one of the most artistically respected independent labels in the world. Blackwell sold Island to PolyGram in 1989; it is now part of Universal Music Group. Island Records' Jamaica-to-world journey is one of the music industry's most extraordinary stories of cultural vision and commercial success.
